days.title: Scoping and Designing a GenAI Solution

concepts.heading: Requirements-First Solution Design
concepts.body: Before selecting a foundation model or drafting an architecture diagram, a GenAI solution design must start from explicit business requirements: required accuracy or quality bar, acceptable latency, cost ceiling per request or per month, and regulatory or compliance constraints such as data residency. These requirements drive every downstream decision, including which model family is viable, whether retrieval or fine-tuning is needed, and what guardrails must be in place. Skipping this step is a common exam trap: a question that jumps straight to 'which model should you pick' is testing whether you recognize that model selection is a consequence of requirements, not a starting point. A documented requirements set also becomes the baseline against which you later measure whether the deployed solution actually succeeded.

concepts.heading: The Generative AI Lens on Well-Architected
concepts.body: AWS extends the six pillars of the Well-Architected Framework (operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization, and sustainability) with a Generative AI Lens that adds GenAI-specific considerations: model selection and lifecycle management, data governance for training and retrieval data, and responsible AI practices such as bias mitigation and content safety. The AWS Well-Architected Tool runs a structured review against this lens, surfacing risks like missing guardrails or unbounded cost per token before they become production incidents. On the exam, a formal architecture review or audit checklist scenario usually points to the Well-Architected Tool and its Generative AI Lens rather than an ad hoc review.

concepts.heading: Validating Feasibility with a PoC
concepts.body: A Proof-of-Concept is a deliberately narrow-scope build meant to test one core hypothesis quickly and cheaply, most often whether a given foundation model can perform a specific domain task well enough to justify further investment. Amazon Bedrock's model playground supports this by letting you prompt different foundation models interactively, without provisioning any infrastructure, so you can compare outputs side by side in minutes. A PoC intentionally defers concerns like scaling, cost optimization, and full guardrail coverage, since its only job is to answer a yes/no question about feasibility. If a scenario says 'quickly validate whether an FM fits before investing in a full build,' a Bedrock playground-driven PoC is almost always the intended answer over a full production deployment.

concepts.heading: Standardizing Reusable Architecture Patterns
concepts.body: Once a pattern works, organizations should standardize it into a reusable template — a RAG pipeline reference architecture, a common agent orchestration pattern, or a shared prompt-management setup — so other teams do not reinvent it from scratch. Standardization reduces duplicated engineering effort, creates a consistent security and governance posture across teams, and shortens the time to bring new GenAI use cases to production. This is distinct from a PoC: a PoC proves an idea works once, while a standardized pattern makes that proven idea repeatable and supportable at scale. Exam questions about consistency across multiple teams building similar GenAI features point to this reuse-and-standardization concept rather than to any single AWS service.

examPoints: When a scenario describes a GenAI project just getting started, the correct first step is defining business requirements (accuracy, latency, cost, compliance) before any architecture or model decision.
When a scenario needs to quickly validate whether a given foundation model fits a domain task before larger investment, a small-scope PoC using the Bedrock playground is the expected answer.

quiz.q: A team is about to start a new GenAI project and is debating whether to begin by selecting a foundation model or by documenting requirements. What should they do first, and why?
choices: Select the foundation model first, since requirements can be adjusted later
Document business requirements (accuracy, latency, cost, compliance) first, since they determine which model and architecture are viable
Build the full production architecture first to see what works
Skip requirements gathering and go straight to a PoC
quiz.explain: Requirements should be defined before model selection because they determine which models, architectures, and guardrails are even viable candidates; picking a model first risks choosing one that doesn't fit the real constraints.

quiz.q: A team wants to quickly determine whether a specific foundation model can handle a specialized legal-summarization task before committing further engineering effort. What is the most efficient approach?
choices: Deploy a full production system immediately
Run a small-scope PoC using the Bedrock model playground to test the hypothesis
Skip evaluation and assume the largest available model will work
Wait until the model has been fine-tuned before testing anything
quiz.explain: A PoC using the Bedrock playground validates the core hypothesis quickly and cheaply without provisioning infrastructure; deploying a full production system first reverses the correct order of validation and investment.

days.recap: Day 1 established that GenAI solution design starts from explicit business requirements, that the Well-Architected Generative AI Lens adds model, data-governance, and responsible-AI considerations, that a PoC validates feasibility cheaply via the Bedrock playground, and that proven patterns should be standardized for reuse across teams.

days.title: Selecting and Orchestrating Foundation Models on Bedrock

concepts.heading: Foundation Model Selection Criteria
concepts.body: Choosing a foundation model means comparing task fit (text generation, summarization, code, multimodal), context window size, per-token cost, latency, and whether the provider supports fine-tuning, all against your Day 1 requirements. Amazon Bedrock exposes multiple model providers — including Anthropic's Claude family and Amazon's own Titan and Nova models — behind a single unified API, so switching providers does not require rewriting your integration code. A larger context window lets you pack more retrieved content or conversation history into a single call but generally costs more per request and can add latency. The exam expects you to match a stated requirement, such as lowest cost per request for simple classification, to the model tier that satisfies it rather than defaulting to the most capable model.

concepts.heading: Dynamic Model Routing by Request Complexity
concepts.body: Rather than sending every request to the same expensive, high-capability model, a dynamic routing architecture classifies incoming requests by complexity or urgency and sends simple ones to a small, cheap model while reserving a larger model for requests that need deep reasoning. AWS AppConfig stores the routing rules and thresholds as external configuration, so the routing logic can be tuned or rolled back instantly without redeploying application code. This pattern directly reduces cost at scale because most real-world traffic skews toward simpler requests. On the exam, phrases like 'route based on request complexity without redeploying' point specifically to AppConfig-driven dynamic routing rather than a hardcoded conditional in application code.

concepts.heading: Resilient Failover with Step Functions
concepts.body: Production GenAI systems must tolerate a primary model being throttled, degraded, or temporarily unavailable, and AWS Step Functions is well suited to encode that failover logic as an explicit state machine: try the primary model, catch a throttling or service exception, and branch to a secondary model or an alternate Region. Because the failover path is defined declaratively rather than buried in application code, it is easier to test, audit, and reason about during an incident. This differs from simple client-side retries, which only reissue the same request to the same endpoint. When a scenario describes automatic fallback to an alternate model or Region after a failure, Step Functions orchestration is the expected answer.

concepts.heading: The FM Customization Spectrum
concepts.body: Foundation model customization exists on a spectrum ordered by cost and effort: prompt engineering is fastest and cheapest and should be tried first, retrieval-augmented generation adds external knowledge without touching model weights, fine-tuning adjusts model weights for domain-specific tone or task performance, and continued pretraining is the most expensive and time-consuming option, reserved for deep domain adaptation at scale. A common exam trap is jumping straight to fine-tuning when the underlying problem is really a knowledge gap that RAG would solve more cheaply. Understanding this ordering lets you eliminate over-engineered answer choices quickly: if a scenario can be solved with a better prompt or added retrieval, that should be preferred over retraining a model.

examPoints: When a scenario needs requests routed to a cheap small model or an expensive large model automatically based on complexity, dynamic routing configured through AWS AppConfig is the keyword to recognize.
When a scenario needs automatic fallback to an alternate model or Region after a primary model call is throttled or fails, Step Functions-based failover orchestration is the expected answer.

quiz.q: A workload needs simple requests routed to a low-cost small model and complex requests routed to a high-performance model, with the ability to change the routing thresholds instantly without a deployment. What should be used?
choices: Always call the same model regardless of complexity
Dynamic routing with thresholds stored in AWS AppConfig
Hardcode the routing logic directly in application code
quiz.explain: AppConfig lets routing rules be updated instantly without redeploying code, which matches the requirement; hardcoding the logic would require a code deployment for every threshold change.

quiz.q: A team needs FM calls to automatically fail over to a secondary model or Region when the primary model is throttled. What should orchestrate this failover logic?
choices: A simple client-side retry to the same endpoint
AWS Step Functions with an explicit failover state machine
Ignoring the failure and returning an error to the user
quiz.explain: Step Functions can declaratively define catch-and-branch failover logic to a secondary model or Region; a simple retry to the same endpoint does not help if that endpoint is the one being throttled.

days.recap: Day 2 covered foundation model selection criteria against Day 1 requirements, dynamic complexity-based routing via AppConfig, resilient failover orchestration with Step Functions, and the prompt-engineering-to-continued-pretraining customization spectrum.

days.title: Customizing Foundation Models and Managing Their Lifecycle

concepts.heading: Fine-Tuning vs. RAG: Choosing the Right Fix
concepts.body: Fine-tuning and RAG solve different problems and the exam tests this distinction relentlessly: choose fine-tuning when you need to change how the model responds — its tone, format, domain vocabulary, or task-specific behavior — and choose RAG when the model's underlying knowledge is missing or outdated, such as internal policy documents it was never trained on. The two are not mutually exclusive; a domain-specific chatbot might use a fine-tuned model for consistent brand voice on top of a RAG pipeline for current facts. A frequent wrong-answer trap is fine-tuning a model to 'teach' it new facts, which is inefficient and prone to becoming stale compared to simply retrieving current documents at query time.

concepts.heading: Bedrock Custom Models and Provisioned Capacity
concepts.body: Amazon Bedrock lets you fine-tune or continue pretraining a foundation model on your own data to create a private custom model that only your account can access. Because a customized model requires dedicated capacity, Bedrock deploys it behind Provisioned Throughput rather than the shared on-demand pool used by base models, which means there is a commitment and cost implication even before the first inference call. This separation matters operationally: teams sometimes forget that a fine-tuned model cannot simply be called on-demand and must be provisioned first, causing an unexpected cost or a failed deployment when that step is skipped.

concepts.heading: Governing Models with SageMaker Model Registry
concepts.body: SageMaker Model Registry provides a structured, versioned catalog for models — recording approval status, lineage back to the training data and job that produced a version, and performance metrics for each candidate. It applies the same governance discipline to fine-tuned foundation models as it traditionally applied to classic ML models, which matters for audits that need to answer which model version was serving production on a given date and who approved it. Registry approval workflows can gate deployment so a new model version cannot reach production without a human sign-off, which is the detail exam questions about controlled model promotion are usually testing.

concepts.heading: The Model Lifecycle Loop
concepts.body: A production GenAI model moves through a repeating cycle of develop, evaluate, approve, deploy, monitor, and retrain, and a new foundation model version should never simply replace an old one without validation. Best practice re-runs the existing prompt suite and evaluation dataset against the new version as a regression test before cutting traffic over, since prompts tuned against one model version can behave differently on the next. This lifecycle discipline is what prevents silent quality regressions when an upstream model provider ships an update. Exam scenarios describing verification that a new model version doesn't degrade existing behavior before rollout are pointing at this regression-testing step.

examPoints: When a scenario states the model must answer using information it was never trained on, such as this week's internal policy update, the correct answer is RAG rather than fine-tuning, because RAG solves a knowledge gap rather than a behavioral one.

When a scenario asks to make responses consistently follow a specific tone, format, or domain vocabulary, the correct answer is fine-tuning, since that changes how the model behaves rather than what it knows.

quiz.q: A support team wants a GenAI assistant to always answer using the company's most recent product recall notices, published as new PDF documents each week. Which approach should the engineer implement?
choices: Fine-tune the foundation model weekly on the new PDFs
Connect a RAG pipeline that retrieves from an up-to-date document store
Switch to a larger foundation model
quiz.explain: RAG retrieves the latest documents at query time without retraining, which fits a knowledge source that changes weekly; weekly fine-tuning would be costly, slow, and quickly stale again as soon as the next notice is published.

quiz.q: An engineering team fine-tuned a foundation model on Bedrock for a specialized legal-drafting task. What must happen before the model can serve production traffic?
choices: Nothing extra — custom models are automatically callable on-demand
The custom model must be deployed with Provisioned Throughput
The model must be re-uploaded to SageMaker Model Registry only
The model must be converted into a classic ML model
quiz.explain: Bedrock custom models require dedicated Provisioned Throughput rather than the shared on-demand pool; SageMaker Model Registry is useful for governance but is not what makes the model invocable.

days.recap: Day 3 established the fine-tuning-versus-RAG decision rule (behavior change vs. knowledge gap), how Bedrock custom models require Provisioned Throughput, and how Model Registry plus regression testing govern the model lifecycle.

days.title: Building Data Validation and Multimodal Ingestion Pipelines

concepts.heading: Automated Data Quality Rules with Glue Data Quality
concepts.body: AWS Glue Data Quality lets you define machine-readable rules for completeness, accuracy, and consistency, then evaluate incoming datasets against those rules automatically as part of an ETL job or pipeline stage. This matters for GenAI specifically because the classic garbage-in-garbage-out problem is amplified when low-quality source data is embedded into a vector store or used to fine-tune a model: the flaws get baked into every downstream response. Rules can be configured to fail the pipeline, quarantine bad records, or simply emit a quality score, giving teams flexibility in how strict data intake should be. A scenario emphasizing automated, rule-based validation of data quality before it reaches a GenAI pipeline points directly at Glue Data Quality.

concepts.heading: Preprocessing Multimodal Inputs
concepts.body: Text, images, audio, and tabular data each need different preprocessing before they are useful to a foundation model or a retrieval pipeline: images are typically captioned or OCR'd into text, audio is transcribed into text using a service like Amazon Transcribe, and tabular data is normalized into a consistent schema so downstream tooling can reason about it uniformly. Treating every modality the same way is a common design mistake, since an FM generally reasons over text, or requires a specific multimodal input format, not raw bytes. Recognizing which preprocessing step converts a given modality into a usable form is exactly what exam questions about multimodal ingestion are testing.

concepts.heading: Lambda-Based Validation Checkpoints
concepts.body: Inserting AWS Lambda functions between pipeline stages provides lightweight, event-driven validation checkpoints that check schema conformance or data format each time a record moves forward, without standing up a persistent validation service. When validation fails, the function can halt the pipeline, route the record to a quarantine location for manual review, or trigger an alert, keeping bad data from silently propagating further downstream. This pattern is cheap to implement and scales naturally with the pipeline's event volume since Lambda runs on demand. It complements Glue Data Quality's broader rule engine by handling narrower, per-stage checks close to where data actually moves.

concepts.heading: Data Quality as the First Line of AI Safety
concepts.body: Poor-quality training or retrieval data is one of the most direct causes of hallucination and biased output in a GenAI system, because a model or retriever can only be as accurate as what it was given to learn from or search over. This makes data pipeline quality control a safety control, not merely a data-engineering nicety — a well-designed Guardrails configuration downstream cannot fully compensate for systematically wrong or biased source data. Teams that treat data quality gates as optional often discover the problem only after users report confidently wrong answers. Exam scenarios connecting reduced hallucination to an upstream fix, rather than a downstream filter, usually intend a data quality improvement.

examPoints: When a scenario needs automatic, rule-based checks for completeness and accuracy applied to data entering a GenAI pipeline, AWS Glue Data Quality is the keyword to recognize over manual or ad hoc review.
When a scenario needs audio content converted into text before it can be used by a GenAI pipeline, Amazon Transcribe is the expected answer rather than a general-purpose NLP or image tool.

quiz.q: A company ingests thousands of scanned PDF invoices per day into a GenAI document pipeline and wants to automatically reject batches with excessive missing fields before they are embedded. What should they implement?
choices: Manually review every batch before ingestion
Define AWS Glue Data Quality rules for completeness and route failing batches for review
Reduce the chunk size used for embeddings
quiz.explain: Glue Data Quality rules for completeness can automatically catch and quarantine bad batches before ingestion; a larger context window or smaller chunks does nothing to fix upstream data completeness.

quiz.q: A GenAI pipeline needs to convert customer service call recordings into text before running them through summarization. Which service should be used first?
quiz.explain: Amazon Transcribe converts audio to text, which is the necessary first step; Comprehend operates on text that already exists rather than on raw audio.

days.recap: Day 4 covered automated data-quality gating with Glue Data Quality, modality-specific preprocessing for multimodal pipelines, Lambda-based per-stage validation, and why upstream data quality is itself an AI-safety control.

days.title: Standardizing FM Input Formats and Cleaning Data for Ingestion

concepts.heading: Prompt Format Differences Across Providers
concepts.body: Every foundation model provider has its own conventions for structuring a prompt — how system, user, and assistant roles are delimited, maximum token limits, and special tokens — which means code written directly against one provider's raw API often breaks when you switch models. Amazon Bedrock's unified Converse API abstracts these differences behind a single, consistent request and response shape, so an application can switch model providers with minimal code changes. This is especially valuable when a dynamic routing architecture sends the same logical request to different underlying models. Exam scenarios about managing prompt format consistency across multiple providers point to the Converse API rather than a provider-specific SDK.

concepts.heading: Enriching Text with Amazon Comprehend
concepts.body: Amazon Comprehend extracts named entities, sentiment, and language identification from raw text, turning unstructured content into structured metadata that a downstream pipeline can use for filtering, routing, or context enrichment. Tagging extracted organization and person names, for example, lets a retrieval system later filter search results by entity, improving relevance beyond plain keyword or vector similarity. Comprehend's language detection is also useful for routing non-English content to an appropriate translation or model path before it reaches an English-optimized FM. When a scenario needs automatic entity extraction to power search filters, Comprehend's named entity recognition is the intended answer.

concepts.heading: Cleaning and Normalizing Data Before Ingestion
concepts.body: Before text enters an embedding or fine-tuning pipeline, common cleanup steps include deduplication, to avoid the same content skewing search relevance or training weight, stripping noise like HTML tags and boilerplate, and masking personally identifiable information proactively rather than after the fact. Deduplication is particularly important for retrieval quality: if the same paragraph appears in multiple near-identical source documents, a vector search can return several redundant hits instead of diverse, useful context. Doing this cleanup once at ingestion time is far cheaper than trying to filter noisy output later at query time.

concepts.heading: Monitoring the Preprocessing Pipeline
concepts.body: Amazon CloudWatch metrics on each preprocessing stage — throughput, failure rate, and latency — let a team catch pipeline bottlenecks early, such as a Comprehend batch job silently falling behind or a Transcribe job queue building up. Without this instrumentation, a slowdown in one stage often only becomes visible once end users notice stale or missing content in the GenAI application. Alarms tied to these metrics, for example a failure rate exceeding a threshold, allow the team to intervene before a backlog becomes a customer-facing incident, rather than discovering the problem retroactively in a postmortem.

examPoints: When multiple FM providers are in use and prompt format needs to be unified into one consistent interface, Bedrock's Converse API is the keyword to look for.
When a scenario needs person or organization names automatically extracted from free text to drive search filters, Amazon Comprehend's named entity recognition is the expected answer.

quiz.q: A team's application currently calls each FM provider's native API directly, and switching providers requires rewriting significant integration code. What should they adopt to reduce this coupling?
choices: A separate SDK per provider maintained in parallel
Amazon Bedrock's Converse API as a unified interface
A custom translation layer written from scratch
quiz.explain: The Converse API is purpose-built to abstract prompt format differences across providers behind one interface, which is exactly the coupling problem described; hand-rolling a translation layer duplicates work AWS already provides.

quiz.q: A company wants to automatically tag customer feedback text with the organizations and products mentioned, to use as search filters later. Which service should they use?
quiz.explain: Comprehend's NER extracts entities like organizations and products from text; Transcribe converts audio to text but does not extract entities, and Macie focuses on sensitive-data discovery.

days.recap: Day 5 covered abstracting prompt formats with the Converse API, enriching text with Comprehend's NER, sentiment, and language detection, ingestion-time cleanup, and monitoring preprocessing pipelines with CloudWatch.

days.title: Designing Vector Store Architectures for RAG

concepts.heading: Choosing a Vector Store
concepts.body: The right vector store depends on what else your data needs to do: Amazon OpenSearch Service combines large-scale k-NN vector search with full-text search in one engine, making it strong when you need both semantic and keyword search together; Amazon RDS or Aurora with the pgvector extension keeps vectors alongside your existing relational data, convenient when vector search must be joined with transactional records; and DynamoDB is not itself a vector engine but excels at storing metadata, conversation history, and session state alongside a dedicated vector store. A common exam trap is picking DynamoDB alone for a vector search requirement — it needs to be paired with an actual vector index to fulfill that role.

concepts.heading: Fully Managed RAG with Bedrock Knowledge Bases
concepts.body: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases automates the entire RAG pipeline — document ingestion, chunking, embedding generation, storage into a vector backend, and query-time retrieval — behind a managed service, removing the need to hand-build each stage. It supports multiple vector store backends including OpenSearch Serverless, Aurora, and third-party options like Pinecone, so teams can pick the backend that matches their existing infrastructure while still getting the managed ingestion and retrieval layer. This is the answer whenever a scenario asks for the fastest way to stand up a working RAG system without building custom ETL and embedding code.

concepts.heading: Metadata Design for Filtering and Security
concepts.body: Storing metadata alongside each vector — source document, access permissions, timestamps, and domain tags — lets a query filter results by more than semantic similarity alone, which is essential for both relevance and security. Filtering by an access-permission tag, for example, ensures a search only returns documents the requesting user is actually authorized to see, preventing a RAG system from leaking restricted content through retrieval. Without a metadata framework, you would either run separate vector indexes per permission level or risk exposing unauthorized content. Exam scenarios about restricting RAG results to certain departments or roles point to metadata-based filtering rather than a separate index per group.

concepts.heading: Tuning Vector Search for Performance
concepts.body: High-performance vector search involves tuning index algorithm parameters such as HNSW's ef_search and M values, choosing a sharding strategy for large collections, and accepting approximate nearest neighbor search as a deliberate accuracy-for-speed tradeoff rather than exact search. Approximate search returns very likely nearest neighbors far faster than an exhaustive scan, which is the right tradeoff for most RAG use cases where a slightly imperfect top-k is acceptable. Getting these parameters wrong shows up as either unacceptably slow queries or degraded relevance, so this tuning is an ongoing operational responsibility, not a one-time setup task.

examPoints: When a scenario wants to stand up document ingestion, chunking, embedding, storage, and retrieval quickly without custom-building each stage, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the keyword to recognize.
When a scenario needs vector search results restricted to only the documents a given department or role is authorized to see, metadata-based access-permission filtering is the expected answer.

quiz.q: A company wants to quickly stand up a RAG system that ingests PDFs from S3, chunks and embeds them, and serves retrieval queries, without building custom ETL and embedding code. What should they use?
choices: A custom Lambda-based ETL pipeline written from scratch
DynamoDB alone as the vector store
quiz.explain: Bedrock Knowledge Bases automates the full RAG pipeline end-to-end; DynamoDB alone cannot perform vector similarity search, and Macie is for sensitive-data discovery, not retrieval.

quiz.q: A RAG-powered internal assistant must ensure that finance-department documents never appear in search results for employees outside that department. What is the most effective way to enforce this?
choices: Train a separate model for each department
Tag vectors with access-permission metadata and filter at query time
Rely on prompt instructions telling the model not to share the content
Disable retrieval entirely for sensitive documents
quiz.explain: Metadata-based filtering enforces access control structurally at the retrieval layer; relying on prompt instructions alone is unreliable and does not prevent the content from being retrieved in the first place.

days.recap: Day 6 compared vector store options (OpenSearch, RDS/Aurora pgvector, DynamoDB for metadata), introduced Bedrock Knowledge Bases as a fully managed RAG pipeline, and covered metadata-driven filtering and HNSW/ANN performance tuning.

days.title: Keeping Vector Data Fresh — Sync, Deletion, and Drift

concepts.heading: Incremental Sync for Cost-Efficient Updates
concepts.body: When new or changed documents land in an S3-backed data source, Bedrock Knowledge Bases can run an incremental sync that only re-embeds the changed portions rather than reprocessing the entire corpus, which dramatically cuts embedding cost and sync time for large, frequently updated document sets. This matters at scale: reprocessing millions of unchanged documents every time a handful of new files arrive would be wasteful and slow. Recognizing 'sync only what changed' as the requirement in a scenario should point you to incremental sync rather than a full re-ingestion job.

concepts.heading: Event-Driven vs. Scheduled Reindexing
concepts.body: Data sources with a strict freshness requirement should reindex via an event-driven path — an S3 event triggering a Lambda function that immediately kicks off a sync — so new content becomes searchable within moments of being uploaded. Data sources where near-real-time freshness is not critical can instead use a periodic scheduled sync, which is simpler to operate and reduces unnecessary sync overhead. Choosing the wrong strategy either wastes compute on unnecessary frequent syncs or leaves users searching stale content when they expected immediacy.

concepts.heading: Preventing Orphaned Vectors on Deletion
concepts.body: When a source document is deleted from S3, its corresponding vectors must also be removed from the index; otherwise the vector store retains orphaned vectors that keep surfacing content from documents that no longer exist, degrading both relevance and trust in the system. Bedrock Knowledge Bases' sync process handles this deletion propagation automatically as part of normal sync operation, which is a detail worth remembering since a naive custom pipeline might only handle additions and updates while forgetting deletions entirely. A scenario describing search results referencing content that was supposedly removed is describing an orphaned-vector problem.

concepts.heading: Detecting and Correcting Embedding Drift
concepts.body: Over time, either the embedding model itself gets updated or the underlying data distribution shifts, causing older vectors and newly generated vectors to become subtly inconsistent with each other — a phenomenon called embedding drift that silently degrades retrieval quality without any obvious error. The fix is periodic full re-sync, re-embedding the entire corpus with the current embedding model, rather than only ever running incremental syncs, since incremental sync alone will never correct vectors that were embedded under an older model version. Recognizing search quality that has quietly degraded over months without any code changes as a symptom of drift, rather than a bug, is the exam-relevant insight here.

examPoints: When a scenario wants only the changed portion of a large document set re-embedded to save cost, incremental sync is the keyword rather than a full reprocessing job.

When a scenario describes search results still referencing documents that have already been deleted, the issue is orphaned vectors, and the fix is ensuring deletion propagates through the sync process.

quiz.q: A knowledge base ingests thousands of documents, and only a handful change each day. Which sync strategy minimizes re-embedding cost?
choices: Full re-sync of the entire corpus every day
Incremental sync of only the changed documents
quiz.explain: Incremental sync re-embeds only what changed, which is far cheaper than reprocessing the full corpus daily; disabling sync would leave the index stale.

quiz.q: Users report that a RAG assistant occasionally cites a document that was deleted from the source S3 bucket weeks ago. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Orphaned vectors were not removed when the source document was deleted
The chunk size is too small
The FM's temperature is set too high
quiz.explain: If the sync process did not propagate the deletion, the vector for that document remains searchable — an orphaned vector; temperature and chunk size do not explain a deleted document still being cited.

days.recap: Day 7 covered incremental sync for cost-efficient updates, choosing event-driven versus scheduled reindexing based on freshness needs, preventing orphaned vectors on deletion, and diagnosing embedding drift with periodic full re-sync.

days.title: Designing the Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipeline

concepts.heading: Chunking Strategy and Its Effect on Retrieval Quality
concepts.body: How you split documents into chunks materially affects retrieval quality: fixed-size chunking is simple to implement but can cut sentences or ideas in half, breaking context; semantic chunking splits along meaning boundaries and generally preserves context better at the cost of more complex preprocessing; and hierarchical chunking preserves document structure so retrieval can reason about where a chunk sits in the larger document. Chunk size and the overlap between adjacent chunks are both tunable and have a real effect on relevance — too small loses context, too large dilutes relevance with unrelated content. A scenario describing retrieved chunks that cut off mid-thought is pointing at a fixed-size chunking problem best solved with semantic chunking or larger overlap.

concepts.heading: Choosing an Embedding Model
concepts.body: Amazon Titan Embeddings offers multilingual support and integrates directly with Bedrock, making it a convenient default choice for many RAG pipelines, but embedding model choice still involves a real tradeoff: higher-dimensional embeddings capture more nuance but cost more to store and compare at query time. Domain-specific applications such as legal, medical, or highly technical fields sometimes benefit from a specialized or fine-tuned embedding model rather than a general-purpose one, since general embeddings may not capture fine distinctions in specialized vocabulary. This dimension-versus-cost tradeoff is the detail exam questions about embedding model selection are usually probing.

concepts.heading: Hybrid Search: Combining Semantic and Keyword Matching
concepts.body: Pure semantic vector search is excellent at capturing conceptual similarity but can underperform on queries containing exact identifiers — product codes, proper nouns, or code snippets — where a keyword-based approach like BM25 full-text search is more precise. Hybrid search runs both approaches and combines their results, covering cases that need exact-match precision alongside cases that need conceptual similarity. This is the answer whenever a scenario needs both finding documents about a general topic and finding documents that mention an exact SKU to work well in the same system.

concepts.heading: Reranking and Query Transformation
concepts.body: A first-pass retrieval step often returns a reasonably relevant but imperfectly ordered set of candidates; a reranking model re-scores those candidates specifically for relevance to the query, typically improving the ordering of the top results that actually get passed to the FM. Separately, query rewriting or expansion techniques — including HyDE, or Hypothetical Document Embeddings, which generates a hypothetical answer and embeds that instead of the raw query — can improve retrieval when the user's literal wording poorly matches the vocabulary of the source documents. These two techniques are complementary: query transformation improves what gets searched for, while reranking improves how the results are ordered afterward.

examPoints: When a scenario needs both exact keyword or code matching and conceptual semantic similarity in the same search, hybrid search combining vector and keyword retrieval is the keyword to recognize.

When a scenario wants the top retrieved results re-scored for relevance before being passed to the model, reranking is the expected answer rather than simply increasing the number of retrieved chunks.

quiz.q: A RAG system frequently fails to retrieve the right document when users search for an exact product SKU, even though semantic search works well for general topic questions. What should be added?
choices: Add hybrid search combining keyword (BM25) and vector search
quiz.explain: Hybrid search adds exact keyword matching alongside semantic search, which is exactly what's missing for exact-identifier queries; increasing embedding dimension does not fix exact-match precision.

quiz.q: After retrieval, the top results are relevant but not well-ordered by actual usefulness to the question. What technique directly addresses this?
quiz.explain: Reranking re-scores already-retrieved candidates specifically for relevance and reorders them; the other options affect what gets retrieved, not how the retrieved set is ordered.

days.recap: Day 8 covered chunking strategy tradeoffs, embedding model selection with Titan Embeddings and the dimension-cost tradeoff, hybrid search for exact-match plus semantic queries, and reranking and query transformation techniques like HyDE.

days.title: Prompt Engineering Strategy and Governance

concepts.heading: Structuring Instructions with System Prompts and Few-Shot Examples
concepts.body: A system prompt establishes the model's role, constraints, and required output format up front, giving the model consistent grounding before it sees any user input, while few-shot examples demonstrate the exact input-output pattern you want by showing worked examples directly in the prompt. Few-shot prompting is especially effective for getting a consistent output format, such as a specific JSON shape, without needing to fine-tune the model. Zero-shot prompting, asking without examples, is faster to write and cheaper in tokens but less reliable when the desired output format is unusual or highly specific.

concepts.heading: Centralized Prompt Versioning with Prompt Management
concepts.body: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management stores prompt templates centrally, supports variables so the same template can be reused across contexts, and versions changes so a prompt can be updated without redeploying application code. This also enables controlled A/B testing between prompt versions to measure which performs better against real traffic before fully rolling out a change. Without centralized management, prompt changes tend to get hardcoded across multiple services, making a simple wording fix require multiple code deployments — exactly the pain point Prompt Management is designed to eliminate.

concepts.heading: Advanced Prompting Techniques
concepts.body: Chain-of-Thought prompting asks the model to reason step by step before producing a final answer, which measurably improves accuracy on multi-step reasoning or math-like problems compared to asking for the answer directly. Self-consistency extends this by generating multiple independent reasoning paths and taking the majority answer, trading extra inference cost for higher reliability on hard problems. These techniques sit on top of the basic few-shot/zero-shot choice and should be reached for specifically when a task requires genuine multi-step reasoning rather than simple lookup or classification.

concepts.heading: Visual Prompt Orchestration with Prompt Flows
concepts.body: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Flows lets you design a multi-step prompt system, including branching and conditional logic that chains multiple prompts or model calls together, as a visual flow rather than hand-written orchestration code. This lowers the engineering effort to build multi-step GenAI logic and, importantly, lets each step in the flow apply its own Guardrails configuration, so safety checks can be enforced at every stage of a complex pipeline rather than only at the very end. Scenarios describing a visual, branching multi-step prompt pipeline with per-step safety enforcement are describing Prompt Flows.

examPoints: When a scenario needs prompt templates centrally versioned and updated without redeploying code, Bedrock Prompt Management is the keyword to recognize, especially if A/B testing between prompt versions is mentioned.
When a scenario requires the model to reason step by step to improve accuracy on a complex, multi-step problem, Chain-of-Thought prompting is the expected answer.

quiz.q: A team wants to update a prompt's wording used across five microservices without redeploying any of them. What should they use?
choices: Hardcode the new wording in each service and redeploy
Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with centrally versioned templates
Increase the model's max token limit
Switch to a different foundation model
quiz.explain: Prompt Management centralizes and versions prompt templates so a change propagates without redeploying application code; hardcoding requires redeploying every service.

quiz.q: A math word-problem solver built on an FM produces frequent calculation errors when asked to answer directly. Which prompting technique is most likely to improve accuracy?
choices: Chain-of-Thought prompting that asks the model to reason step by step
Reducing the prompt to a single word
quiz.explain: Chain-of-Thought prompting improves accuracy on multi-step reasoning tasks like math word problems; increasing temperature would increase randomness, not accuracy.

days.recap: Day 9 covered system prompts and few-shot examples for instruction framing, centralized prompt versioning with Prompt Management, advanced techniques like Chain-of-Thought and self-consistency, and visual multi-step orchestration with Prompt Flows plus per-step Guardrails.

days.title: Domain 1 Review — The FM Integration Pipeline End to End

concepts.heading: The End-to-End Pipeline, in Order
concepts.body: Domain 1 traces one continuous pipeline: define business requirements, select and configure a foundation model, decide how to customize it through prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning, or continued pretraining, build a validated multimodal data pipeline, design and maintain a vector store, assemble the RAG retrieval mechanism, and govern prompts. Because this domain carries the largest exam weight, questions often test whether you can place a described symptom or requirement correctly within this pipeline rather than testing any single service in isolation. When reading a scenario, first identify which stage of this pipeline it describes before trying to recall a specific service name.

concepts.heading: The Fine-Tuning vs. RAG Decision, Revisited
concepts.body: The single most frequently tested distinction in this domain is whether a described problem is a knowledge gap, solved with RAG, or a behavior and style problem, solved with fine-tuning — recognizing which one a scenario describes is often enough to eliminate two of four answer choices immediately. A secondary, closely related test is recognizing when the two should be combined: a fine-tuned model for consistent tone, backed by RAG for current facts, is a legitimate and commonly tested combined pattern rather than an either/or choice.

concepts.heading: Vector Store and Retrieval Quality Levers
concepts.body: Retrieval quality depends on a chain of decisions — chunking strategy, embedding model choice, hybrid search versus pure semantic search, and reranking — and a well-prepared candidate can trace a described symptom, such as irrelevant results, cut-off context, or poor exact-match performance, back to the specific lever that would fix it. Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the default fully-managed, get-this-working-fast answer whenever a scenario does not have a specific reason to hand-build a custom pipeline.

concepts.heading: Data Quality and Vector Freshness as Ongoing Operations
concepts.body: Domain 1 is not only about initial design — data quality gating, incremental sync, orphaned-vector cleanup, and drift detection are ongoing operational responsibilities that keep a RAG system trustworthy over time. A system that was well-designed at launch can still degrade months later if these operational practices are neglected, which is why exam scenarios sometimes describe a system that used to work well and ask what changed — the answer is usually drift, staleness, or a data quality regression rather than a design flaw.

examPoints: In any Domain 1 scenario, first classify it as a knowledge-gap problem (RAG) or a behavior/style problem (fine-tuning) before considering more specific service details.
When a scenario describes retrieval quality that has quietly degraded over time without any code changes, suspect embedding drift or stale vector sync rather than a fundamental architecture flaw.

quiz.q: A support assistant needs to answer using this week's newly published product documentation, which the base model has never seen. Which approach directly solves this?
choices: Fine-tuning the model on the new documentation
Connecting a RAG pipeline that retrieves the new documentation at query time
quiz.explain: This is a knowledge-gap problem, which RAG solves directly by retrieving current content; fine-tuning is slower, costlier, and would need to be repeated every time documentation changes.

quiz.q: Which AWS service provides a fully managed RAG pipeline covering ingestion, chunking, embedding, storage, and retrieval?
quiz.explain: Bedrock Knowledge Bases automates the entire RAG pipeline; the other services support governance, data quality, and monitoring but are not RAG pipelines themselves.

days.recap: Domain 1 review: from requirements through FM selection and customization, data pipeline validation, vector store design, RAG mechanics, and prompt governance — the foundation for building a working GenAI solution end to end.

days.title: Building Agentic AI Solutions with the ReAct Pattern

concepts.heading: What Makes an AI System Agentic
concepts.body: An agentic AI system goes beyond answering a single question: it autonomously plans a sequence of steps, calls external tools to gather information or take action, observes the results, and decides what to do next, repeating until it reaches a goal. This is a fundamentally different architecture from a single-turn Q&A model, since the system now needs state tracking across multiple steps and a mechanism to decide when it is actually done. Recognizing multi-step, autonomous, decides-what-to-do-next-based-on-results as the defining signature of agentic AI is what separates it from simple prompt-response usage in exam scenarios.

concepts.heading: The ReAct Loop: Reason, Act, Observe
concepts.body: ReAct, short for Reasoning plus Acting, structures an agent's behavior as a repeating loop: the model reasons about what it needs to do next, takes an action such as calling a tool, observes the result of that action, and feeds that observation back into the next reasoning step, continuing until the goal is met. This is effectively Chain-of-Thought reasoning combined with the ability to act on the world rather than only think about it. A scenario describing an agent that must call an external API, look at the result, and decide on a next step based on that result is describing the ReAct pattern specifically.

concepts.heading: Short-Term vs. Long-Term Agent Memory
concepts.body: An agent's short-term memory holds the current conversation context and recent action history for the duration of a session, while long-term memory persists information — user preferences, past interactions, prior task outcomes — across sessions, typically backed by a durable store like DynamoDB. Choosing the wrong memory strategy causes predictable failures: an agent using only short-term memory forgets a user between sessions, while over-reliance on long-term memory without proper scoping can leak context between unrelated conversations. A scenario requiring an agent to recall something after the session ended points specifically to long-term, persisted memory.

concepts.heading: Building Agents Quickly with Strands Agents
concepts.body: Strands Agents is AWS's framework for defining an agent's model, available tools, and prompting concisely in code, letting teams assemble a working agent quickly instead of hand-building the ReAct loop, tool-calling glue, and state management from scratch. It reduces boilerplate specifically around tool invocation and response parsing, which are the parts of agent-building that are easy to get subtly wrong. When a scenario emphasizes rapid agent development on AWS without naming a specific low-level orchestration mechanism, Strands Agents is a reasonable default answer.

examPoints: When a scenario describes a system that must reason, call a tool, observe the result, and decide on a next action in a repeating loop, the ReAct pattern is the keyword to recognize.

When a scenario requires an agent to remember something from a conversation that ended, long-term memory backed by a persistent store such as DynamoDB is the expected answer, not session-only short-term memory.

quiz.q: An agent must look up a customer's order status via an API, then decide whether to escalate based on what it finds, repeating this process until the issue is resolved. Which pattern describes this behavior?
quiz.explain: The described reason-act-observe-repeat loop is the defining structure of ReAct; a single synchronous call could not repeat and adapt based on intermediate results.

quiz.q: Users complain that a support agent has no memory of their previous conversation from yesterday. What should be added?
choices: Long-term memory backed by a persistent store like DynamoDB
quiz.explain: Recalling information across sessions requires long-term, persisted memory; a larger context window only helps within a single session and does not persist across sessions.

days.recap: Day 11 introduced agentic AI as autonomous multi-step planning and action, the ReAct reason-act-observe loop, short-term versus long-term memory, and Strands Agents as AWS's framework for building agents quickly.

days.title: Tool Integration, Error Handling, and Human-in-the-Loop Safeguards

concepts.heading: Standardizing Tool Access with MCP
concepts.body: The Model Context Protocol is an open protocol that lets an agent communicate with external tools and data sources in a standardized way; exposing a tool as an MCP server means any MCP-compatible agent framework can call it without custom, framework-specific integration glue. This is valuable in organizations running multiple agent frameworks or expecting to switch frameworks over time, since tools built once as MCP servers remain reusable regardless of which orchestration layer calls them. A scenario emphasizing reuse of the same tool across multiple different agent frameworks is describing exactly the problem MCP solves.

concepts.heading: Handling Tool Failures Gracefully
concepts.body: Tool calls fail for mundane reasons — timeouts, malformed parameters, transient service errors — and a well-designed agent needs a defined response: retry with backoff, fall back to an alternate tool, or surface a clear failure rather than looping indefinitely. A hard cap on the number of iterations or tool calls is essential, since without one a confused agent can loop forever, burning cost and never reaching a useful answer. Exam scenarios describing an agent stuck in an endless retry loop are testing whether you know to add an iteration limit as a structural safeguard, not just better error messages.

concepts.heading: Least-Privilege Guardrails via IAM
concepts.body: The tools an agent is permitted to call should be scoped by IAM policy to the minimum set of actions actually required for its task, following the same least-privilege principle used elsewhere in AWS security — an agent that only needs to read order data should not also hold permission to modify billing records. This limits the blast radius if the agent is manipulated, through prompt injection for example, into attempting an action it should not take, since IAM will simply deny the unauthorized call regardless of what the model decided to do. This is a defense-in-depth layer that works even if upstream prompt-level safeguards fail.

concepts.heading: Human-in-the-Loop for Irreversible Actions
concepts.body: For actions that cannot be undone — issuing a payment, deleting a record, sending an external communication — best practice inserts an explicit human approval step rather than letting the agent execute autonomously, typically implemented with AWS Step Functions' wait-for-callback pattern, which pauses the state machine until a human approves or rejects the pending action. This differs from IAM restriction: IAM prevents unauthorized actions entirely, while human-in-the-loop allows an authorized but high-risk action to proceed only with explicit sign-off. A scenario requiring approval before an irreversible action is executed is describing HITL specifically.

examPoints: When a scenario requires human approval before an agent performs an irreversible action like a payment or deletion, Human-in-the-Loop implemented via Step Functions' wait-for-callback is the keyword to recognize.
When a scenario needs the same tool reused across multiple different agent frameworks without custom integration work for each, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is the expected answer.

quiz.q: A company runs agents on two different orchestration frameworks and wants both to call the same internal inventory-lookup tool without writing separate integration code for each framework. What should they implement?
choices: A separate custom SDK per framework
Expose the tool as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server
Hardcode the tool logic into each agent
quiz.explain: MCP standardizes tool access so any compatible framework can call the same tool without custom per-framework glue; writing a separate SDK per framework duplicates the very work MCP avoids.

quiz.q: An agent is authorized to call a payment-processing tool, and the company wants to ensure no payment executes without a person explicitly approving it first. What should be added to the workflow?
choices: A retry loop with exponential backoff
A Human-in-the-Loop approval step using Step Functions' wait-for-callback pattern
A larger IAM policy granting broader access
quiz.explain: HITL with a wait-for-callback state pauses execution until a human approves the irreversible action; a retry loop addresses transient failures, not the need for human sign-off.

days.recap: Day 12 covered standardizing tool access with MCP, handling tool failures with retries and iteration caps, enforcing least-privilege tool scope via IAM, and requiring human approval for irreversible actions via Step Functions' wait-for-callback pattern.

days.title: Orchestrating Multi-Agent Systems

concepts.heading: Why Split Work Across Multiple Specialized Agents
concepts.body: Rather than building one general-purpose agent that tries to do everything, a multi-agent system splits work across specialized agents — a router, a search specialist, a code-generation specialist — each tuned for its narrow task, with an orchestrator agent integrating their individual outputs into a final response. Specialization tends to improve quality on each sub-task because a narrowly-scoped agent's prompt, tools, and context can be optimized specifically for that job rather than being a compromise across many jobs at once. This pattern is most effective when the overall task can be cleanly decomposed into clearly separable subtasks.

concepts.heading: Intent-Based Routing with Agent Squad
concepts.body: AWS Agent Squad is an orchestration framework that classifies an incoming user request by intent and routes it to the specialized agent best equipped to handle it, for example routing a billing question to a billing-specialist agent and a technical question to a technical-support agent. This intent classification happens before any specialist agent is invoked, so the routing decision itself becomes a discrete, testable step in the pipeline. A scenario describing automatic routing of user requests to the most appropriate specialized agent based on what the user is asking is describing Agent Squad's core function.

concepts.heading: Explicit Orchestration with Step Functions
concepts.body: For multi-agent workflows that need explicit, auditable control over call order, parallel execution, and conditional branching, Step Functions' state machine model provides that visibility directly — you can see exactly which agent ran when, in what order, and why a particular branch was taken, which is invaluable for debugging a complex failure. This differs from letting agents coordinate implicitly through shared memory or ad hoc messaging, which is harder to trace and debug when something goes wrong. Exam scenarios emphasizing visibility and debuggability of a multi-agent workflow's execution order point to Step Functions orchestration.

concepts.heading: The Multi-Agent Tradeoff: Quality vs. Coordination Overhead
concepts.body: Multi-agent systems can improve per-task quality through specialization, but that benefit comes with real costs: inter-agent communication overhead, increased latency from multiple sequential calls, and coordination complexity that grows with the number of agents involved. This pattern is most appropriate when subtasks are clearly separable; forcing a task that is not naturally decomposable into a multi-agent architecture usually adds complexity without a corresponding quality benefit. Recognizing when a single well-designed agent is actually the better answer, rather than defaulting to multi-agent for every complex task, is itself a tested judgment call.

examPoints: When a scenario needs incoming requests automatically routed to the most appropriate specialized agent based on intent, AWS Agent Squad is the keyword to recognize.

When a scenario needs explicit, auditable visibility into multi-agent call order, parallel execution, and branching, Step Functions state machine orchestration is the expected answer over implicit agent-to-agent coordination.

quiz.q: A customer service platform wants incoming chat messages automatically routed to a billing agent, a technical agent, or a returns agent, based on what the customer is asking about. What should they use?
choices: A single general-purpose agent handling all message types
AWS Agent Squad for intent-based routing to specialist agents
quiz.explain: Agent Squad classifies intent and routes to the appropriate specialist agent, which directly matches the requirement; a single general-purpose agent forgoes the specialization benefit entirely.

quiz.q: A team debugging a multi-agent failure needs to see the exact order in which agents were called and why a particular branch was taken. What should the workflow use?
choices: Implicit coordination through shared memory only
Step Functions state machine orchestration with explicit branching
quiz.explain: Step Functions provides explicit, auditable visibility into call order and branching logic, which is exactly what's needed for debugging; implicit shared-memory coordination is much harder to trace.

days.recap: Day 13 covered why to split work across specialized agents, intent-based routing with Agent Squad, explicit and auditable orchestration with Step Functions, and the quality-versus-coordination-overhead tradeoff of multi-agent systems.

days.title: FM Deployment Strategies — Provisioned Throughput and SageMaker Endpoints

concepts.heading: Bedrock On-Demand vs. Provisioned Throughput
concepts.body: On-Demand pricing on Bedrock charges per token used, which fits workloads with variable or unpredictable traffic since you never pay for idle capacity, while Provisioned Throughput reserves a committed level of capacity for a fixed period, which fits predictable, large-scale traffic and is required for serving a custom, fine-tuned or continually pretrained, model at all. This distinction is exam-relevant in both directions: choosing Provisioned Throughput for a low, spiky-traffic workload wastes money on unused reserved capacity, while choosing On-Demand for a large predictable workload with a custom model is often not even an available option.

concepts.heading: SageMaker AI Endpoint Types
concepts.body: SageMaker AI lets you host a self-fine-tuned model or an open-source foundation model directly, choosing among real-time endpoints for continuous, latency-sensitive traffic, serverless endpoints for intermittent traffic where you do not want to pay for idle capacity, and asynchronous endpoints for large-payload or long-running inference where the caller does not need an immediate response. Picking the wrong endpoint type either wastes money on an always-on real-time endpoint serving sporadic traffic, or introduces unacceptable cold-start latency by using serverless for a low-latency, high-throughput requirement.

concepts.heading: Container-Based Deployment and GPU Scaling
concepts.body: Large models are commonly deployed across multiple GPU instances using model parallelism, splitting a single model's weights across several GPUs when it is too large to fit on one, and inference-optimized containers such as DJL or TensorRT-LLM improve both throughput and latency compared to a naive deployment. This level of infrastructure control is specific to self-managed hosting on SageMaker; Bedrock abstracts this complexity away entirely, which is itself a useful signal — a scenario mentioning explicit GPU or container configuration is pointing toward SageMaker rather than Bedrock.

concepts.heading: Matching Deployment Strategy to Workload Characteristics
concepts.body: The right deployment choice is a function of traffic pattern, whether steady, intermittent, or bursty, latency requirement, real-time versus batch-tolerant, cost sensitivity, and how customized the model is — a scenario that specifies several of these dimensions is testing whether you can weigh them together rather than optimizing for just one. Predictable high volume with a custom fine-tuned model clearly points to Bedrock Provisioned Throughput or a SageMaker real-time endpoint, while occasional batch jobs with no latency sensitivity points to a SageMaker asynchronous endpoint.

examPoints: When a scenario describes predictable, large-scale traffic serving a custom fine-tuned model with a stable throughput requirement, Bedrock Provisioned Throughput is the keyword to recognize.
When a scenario describes intermittent traffic where idle cost must be avoided, a SageMaker serverless endpoint is the expected answer over a continuously running real-time endpoint.

quiz.q: A company needs to serve a custom fine-tuned model to a large, predictable volume of enterprise customers at a guaranteed throughput level. Which Bedrock option should they choose?
quiz.explain: Provisioned Throughput reserves guaranteed capacity for predictable, large-scale traffic and is required for serving custom models; On-Demand does not guarantee throughput and is better suited to variable traffic.

quiz.q: A workload calls a self-hosted model only a few times per hour and the team wants to avoid paying for continuously running infrastructure. Which SageMaker endpoint type fits best?
choices: Asynchronous endpoint only for large payloads
A dedicated GPU cluster running continuously
quiz.explain: A serverless endpoint scales to zero and only charges when invoked, which fits low, intermittent call volume; a real-time endpoint or dedicated GPU cluster would incur ongoing idle cost.

days.recap: Day 14 compared Bedrock On-Demand versus Provisioned Throughput, SageMaker's real-time, serverless, and asynchronous endpoint types, container and GPU scaling for large models, and how to match deployment strategy to traffic pattern and cost sensitivity.

days.title: Enterprise Integration — APIs, Events, and Identity

concepts.heading: Exposing GenAI Capability via API Gateway
concepts.body: Amazon API Gateway exposes GenAI functionality as a standard REST or WebSocket API that internal and external systems can call using familiar, well-understood interfaces, while enforcing request validation, throttling to protect downstream capacity, and usage plans that meter and limit consumption per API key or client. This is the standard pattern for making a GenAI feature consumable by other teams' applications without exposing raw model-invocation credentials or internal orchestration details.

concepts.heading: Loosely Coupled Integration with EventBridge
concepts.body: Rather than having downstream systems call a GenAI service directly and wait synchronously for a response, an event-driven integration publishes the result of GenAI processing as an event on Amazon EventBridge, letting multiple independent downstream consumers react to that event without the producing system needing to know who they are. This loose coupling is valuable when a single GenAI output, such as a document classification, needs to trigger several unrelated downstream workflows, since adding a new consumer later requires no change to the producing system at all.

concepts.heading: Enterprise Identity and Access Control
concepts.body: Identity federation integrates enterprise single sign-on via SAML or OIDC so users authenticate with credentials they already have, and role-based access control then limits which GenAI features a given authenticated user or role can actually invoke. Combining these two lets an organization enforce fine-grained, per-user access to GenAI functionality without maintaining a separate credential system just for the AI application. A scenario requiring GenAI feature access scoped by a user's existing corporate identity and role is describing this federation-plus-RBAC pattern.

concepts.heading: The GenAI Gateway Pattern
concepts.body: When multiple teams each call foundation models independently, a centralized GenAI gateway consolidates those calls behind one integration point, enabling unified usage tracking, cost allocation back to individual teams, consistently applied Guardrails across every caller, and centralized model version management. Without a gateway, each team enforces its own possibly inconsistent safety and cost controls, which makes organization-wide governance nearly impossible to audit. A scenario describing the need for consistent safety controls and cost visibility across many teams calling FMs independently is describing the GenAI gateway pattern specifically.

examPoints: When a scenario needs multiple teams' FM usage tracked, cost-allocated, and protected by consistent Guardrails from one central point, the GenAI gateway pattern is the keyword to recognize.
When a scenario needs GenAI feature access scoped by a user's existing corporate SSO identity and role, identity federation combined with RBAC is the expected answer.

quiz.q: An organization has five teams independently calling foundation models with inconsistent safety filtering and no unified cost visibility. What architecture pattern addresses this?
choices: Let each team continue managing its own integration
A centralized GenAI gateway consolidating usage tracking, cost allocation, and Guardrails
Disable FM access for all but one team
quiz.explain: A centralized GenAI gateway provides unified tracking, cost allocation, and consistent safety controls across all teams; letting teams continue independently perpetuates the inconsistency described.

quiz.q: A company wants GenAI feature access limited based on each employee's existing corporate SSO identity and department role. What should they implement?
choices: A separate password system just for the GenAI app
Identity federation with SSO combined with role-based access control
Open access for all authenticated users regardless of role
API keys shared across the whole company
quiz.explain: Federating with existing SSO and layering RBAC on top scopes access by the user's real identity and role; a separate password system duplicates infrastructure unnecessarily.

days.recap: Day 15 covered exposing GenAI via API Gateway with throttling and usage plans, loosely coupled event-driven integration with EventBridge, identity federation plus RBAC, and the centralized GenAI gateway pattern for multi-team governance.

days.title: Hybrid, Edge, and CI/CD for GenAI Workloads

concepts.heading: Running GenAI On-Premises with AWS Outposts
concepts.body: AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure into a customer's own data center, which matters for GenAI workloads subject to data-residency or data-sovereignty rules preventing certain data from ever leaving the premises, since Outposts lets that workload use the same AWS APIs and services it would use in the cloud, just running locally. This avoids having to build an entirely separate, non-AWS on-premises solution just to satisfy a residency constraint. A scenario describing regulatory data-residency requirements that prevent moving data to the cloud, while still wanting AWS-native tooling, is describing an Outposts use case.

concepts.heading: Ultra-Low-Latency Inference at the Edge with Wavelength
concepts.body: AWS Wavelength places compute infrastructure at the edge of telecom 5G networks, enabling GenAI inference with latency low enough to serve mobile and IoT use cases like real-time image recognition, where round-tripping every request to a central Region would introduce unacceptable delay. This is a narrower use case than Outposts: Wavelength solves a latency problem specifically for mobile and edge devices on 5G networks, whereas Outposts solves a data-residency problem for a fixed on-premises location.

concepts.heading: Cross-Environment Architectures: Cloud and Edge Together
concepts.body: A cross-environment GenAI solution combines a large model in the cloud with a lightweight model at the edge, routing simple requests to the edge model for an immediate response and reserving cloud routing only for requests complex enough to need the larger model's capability. This balances latency and cost: most requests get handled cheaply and instantly at the edge, while only the subset that truly needs it incurs the cost and latency of a round trip to the cloud model.

concepts.heading: CI/CD for GenAI Application Changes
concepts.body: A GenAI-specific CI/CD pipeline built with CodePipeline and CodeBuild automatically tests and deploys changes to prompt templates, Guardrails configuration, and agent logic, integrating prompt regression testing directly into the pipeline so a prompt change cannot ship without first being validated against a known evaluation set. This extends familiar software CI/CD discipline to artifacts that are easy to overlook — a wording tweak to a prompt can silently break behavior just as much as a code change can, which is exactly why it needs the same testing rigor.

examPoints: When a scenario describes a data-sovereignty rule preventing certain data from leaving the premises while still wanting AWS-native APIs, AWS Outposts is the keyword to recognize.
When a scenario needs ultra-low-latency real-time inference for mobile or IoT devices on a telecom network, AWS Wavelength is the expected answer rather than a central-Region deployment.

quiz.q: A financial institution must keep certain customer data on-premises due to regulation, but still wants to build its GenAI application using AWS-native services and APIs. What should they use?
choices: Migrate the data to the cloud regardless of regulation
AWS Outposts to run AWS infrastructure on-premises
quiz.explain: Outposts extends AWS infrastructure and APIs into the customer's own data center, satisfying the data-residency requirement; Wavelength addresses mobile-edge latency, not data residency.

quiz.q: A mobile AR application needs real-time GenAI-based image recognition with latency too low to tolerate a round trip to a central AWS Region. What should be used?
quiz.explain: Wavelength places compute at the 5G network edge specifically to serve ultra-low-latency mobile use cases; a standard Regional endpoint would introduce unacceptable round-trip latency.

days.recap: Day 16 covered AWS Outposts for on-premises data-residency needs, AWS Wavelength for ultra-low-latency edge inference, combining cloud and edge models in one architecture, and CI/CD pipelines that regression-test prompts and Guardrails before deployment.

days.title: Robust FM API Integration — Streaming, Backoff, and Routing

concepts.heading: Synchronous vs. Asynchronous FM Invocation
concepts.body: A conversational UI that needs a quick response should call the FM synchronously, while large batch jobs or long-running tasks should be decoupled through an Amazon SQS queue so the caller does not block waiting for a slow response and the system can absorb bursts of requests without overwhelming the model endpoint. This decoupling also improves overall throughput, since a queue lets you control the rate at which requests are actually processed independent of how fast they arrive.

concepts.heading: Real-Time Streaming Responses
concepts.body: Bedrock's streaming API, InvokeModelWithResponseStream, delivers generated tokens to the client as soon as they are produced rather than waiting for the entire response to finish, which meaningfully improves perceived responsiveness — specifically the time-to-first-token — in a chat-style interface even though total generation time may be unchanged. This matters because users judge responsiveness by how quickly something starts appearing, not only by total completion time, so streaming is a UX improvement layered on top of, not a replacement for, backend performance optimization.

concepts.heading: Resilience with Exponential Backoff and Jitter
concepts.body: When an FM call is throttled, retrying immediately at full speed usually just gets throttled again and can make congestion worse; exponential backoff progressively increases the wait time between retry attempts, and adding jitter, a small random variation, prevents many clients from retrying in synchronized waves that recreate the same spike. Rate limiting on the client side further protects downstream systems from being overwhelmed by a client that would otherwise retry too aggressively. This combination is the standard, expected resilience pattern for any throttling-prone API, not just Bedrock specifically.

concepts.heading: Intelligent Routing and Distributed Tracing
concepts.body: Routing requests to the model best suited to their characteristics reduces both cost and latency at scale, and AWS X-Ray provides distributed tracing across the entire request path, including the FM call itself, so a team can pinpoint exactly where latency is accumulating in a multi-step pipeline rather than guessing. Without tracing, diagnosing why a specific request is slow in a system with retrieval, routing, and multiple downstream calls becomes largely guesswork.

examPoints: When a scenario wants tokens shown to the user as soon as they are generated to improve perceived responsiveness, Bedrock's streaming API (InvokeModelWithResponseStream) is the keyword to recognize.
When a scenario describes FM calls being throttled and wants retry intervals that progressively increase rather than retrying immediately, exponential backoff with jitter is the expected answer.

quiz.q: A chat application feels slow to users even though total response generation time hasn't changed, because they wait for the entire answer before anything appears. What should be implemented?
choices: Bedrock's streaming API to deliver tokens as they are generated
quiz.explain: Streaming improves perceived responsiveness by showing tokens as they're generated rather than waiting for full completion; backoff addresses throttling, not perceived latency.

quiz.q: An application's FM calls are frequently throttled, and immediate retries seem to make the throttling worse. What resilience pattern should be applied?
choices: Retry immediately and repeatedly with no delay
Exponential backoff with jitter between retry attempts
Send requests in a tighter loop
quiz.explain: Exponential backoff with jitter spreads out retries and avoids synchronized retry storms, directly addressing the described problem; retrying immediately without delay is what caused it.

days.recap: Day 17 covered synchronous versus SQS-decoupled asynchronous FM calls, streaming responses for perceived speed, exponential backoff with jitter for throttling resilience, and intelligent routing paired with X-Ray tracing for diagnosing latency.

days.title: Application Integration Patterns and Developer Productivity Tools

concepts.heading: Building the Client-Side FM Interface
concepts.body: A production chat UI needs to handle a streaming response as it arrives, rather than only a single completed response, and manage token budget as a conversation grows, summarizing or dropping older messages once the running context approaches the model's context-window limit. Neglecting the second point causes a conversation to eventually fail outright once it exceeds the model's maximum input size, which is a common and avoidable production bug in long-running chat applications.

concepts.heading: Rapid Full-Stack Builds with AWS Amplify
